source_metadata.title: Heparin: Mechanism of Action, Pharmacokinetics, Dosing Considerations, Monitoring, Efficacy, and Safety
source_metadata.source_scope_note: Secondary source. Trial results are represented as the chapter's report of underlying studies and tagged secondary_reported_result; this extraction does not imply that this chapter generated those primary data.

atoms.canonical_statement: The chapter reviews heparin and LMWH mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, anticoagulant effects, laboratory monitoring, and briefly summarizes clinical uses.
Intravenous heparin has an immediate anticoagulant onset and was presented as the anticoagulant of choice when a rapid effect is required.
The chapter distinguishes low-dose heparin for primary prophylaxis from higher therapeutic doses used to prevent recurrent thrombosis.
For long-term anticoagulation with oral anticoagulants, the chapter recommends an approximately 4-day overlap with heparin.
The chapter assigns level I evidence to heparin for prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism and for early treatment of unstable angina.
Heparin is a glycosaminoglycan composed of alternating D-glucosamine and uronic-acid residues.
A high-affinity pentasaccharide sequence that binds antithrombin III is present in approximately one third of heparin molecules.
Heparin binding induces a conformational change in antithrombin III that accelerates inactivation of thrombin, factor Xa, and factor IXa.
Heparin accelerates thrombin inactivation by forming a ternary complex involving heparin, thrombin, and antithrombin III.
Factor Xa inactivation by the heparin-antithrombin complex does not require ternary-complex formation.
Heparin chains shorter than 18 saccharides cannot simultaneously bind thrombin and antithrombin III but can retain factor Xa inhibitory activity.
Heparin can also catalyze thrombin inactivation through heparin cofactor II, an effect requiring substantially higher heparin concentrations than antithrombin-mediated activity.
Unfractionated heparin has a reported molecular-weight range of about 5,000 to 30,000 with a mean near 15,000.
Higher-molecular-weight heparin species are cleared more rapidly than lower-molecular-weight species, contributing to in-vivo enrichment of lower-molecular-weight chains.

The chapter attributes part of the discordance between anti-factor Xa heparin levels and APTT response to accumulation of lower-molecular-weight heparin species with relatively less thrombin activity.
Figure 1 depicts the chain-length requirement for heparin-mediated thrombin inhibition and the absence of that requirement for factor Xa inhibition.
Heparin is not orally absorbed; the chapter identifies IV and subcutaneous administration as preferred routes and advises avoiding intramuscular injection because of hematoma risk.
Intermittent IV heparin administration was reported to be associated with more bleeding than continuous IV infusion.
When immediate anticoagulation is required with subcutaneous heparin, the chapter recommends an IV bolus because the subcutaneous anticoagulant effect is delayed by about 1 to 2 hours.
Heparin binding to plasma proteins is described as contributing to reduced low-concentration bioavailability, variable fixed-dose response, and heparin resistance.
Heparin clearance is described as a combination of rapid saturable cellular clearance and slower nonsaturable clearance that is partly renal.
The apparent biologic half-life of heparin increases with dose, from about 30 minutes after 25 U/kg IV to 60 minutes after 100 U/kg and 150 minutes after 400 U/kg.
Subcutaneous heparin has reduced plasma recovery at low and moderate doses, whereas plasma recovery is reported as nearly complete at therapeutic doses above 35,000 U per 24 hours.
The review reports that at 24 hours therapeutic heparin levels and APTT ratios were achieved in 37% with subcutaneous heparin versus 71% with continuous IV heparin at the same 30,000-U/day dose.

population.label: Patients with venous thrombosis randomized to subcutaneous or continuous IV heparin

concept.text: Therapeutic heparin level and APTT ratio at 24 hours

atoms.canonical_statement: APTT is described as the usual laboratory monitor for therapeutic heparin because it reflects inhibition of thrombin, factor Xa, and factor IXa.
Elevated factor VIII during acute-phase states can reduce the APTT response relative to the circulating heparin level.
The historical APTT ratio target of 1.5 was based on an animal thrombosis model and is not reliably transferable across commercial APTT reagents.
The review reports that five APTT reagents produced therapeutic APTT ratio ranges spanning approximately 1.8-2.5 to 2.6-4.2, so a universal APTT ratio was inappropriate.

population.label: Plasma samples used to compare five commercial APTT reagents

concept.text: APTT ratio corresponding to therapeutic heparin concentrations

quantitative_result.effect_measure: lower bound of reported reagent-specific therapeutic APTT ratio range

atoms.canonical_statement: The chapter recommends calibrating each local APTT reagent to a heparin concentration of 0.2-0.4 U/mL by protamine titration or approximately 0.3-0.7 U/mL by anti-factor Xa assay.
Figure 2 demonstrates substantial reagent-dependent variation in APTT response to the same in-vitro heparin concentrations.
A chromogenic anti-factor Xa assay with a target of 0.3-0.7 U/mL is presented as an alternative method for therapeutic heparin monitoring.
The APTT is described as useful over heparin concentrations around 0.1-1.0 U/mL but often unmeasurably prolonged above 1 U/mL.
For procedures requiring high heparin concentrations, such as cardiac bypass and high-risk angioplasty, the chapter favors activated clotting time over APTT monitoring.
Table 1 reports recurrent VTE in 4/60 patients given 30,000 U/day heparin versus 12/60 patients in a no-heparin lower-dose arm in the Brandjes 1992 study.

population.label: Brandjes et al 1992 VTE trial participants

quantitative_result.effect_measure: recurrent VTE rate in high-dose arm (%)

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 reports recurrent VTE in 3/58 patients receiving continuous IV heparin versus 11/57 receiving subcutaneous heparin in the Hull 1986 study.

population.label: Hull et al 1986 VTE trial participants

atoms.canonical_statement: The Basu prospective cohort reported 5 recurrent VTE events among 162 patients; all five had APTT values below 50 seconds for at least 3 consecutive days before recurrence.

population.label: Basu et al prospective cohort of patients with venous thrombosis

concept.text: Therapeutic unfractionated heparin adjusted by APTT

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 3 summarizes 628 patients receiving at least 30,000 U/day heparin with an overall recurrent VTE rate of 5.7%.

population.label: Patients in contemporary studies receiving at least 30,000 U/day UFH

concept.text: Unfractionated heparin at least 30,000 U/24 h

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that the Raschke weight-based nomogram reduced recurrent thromboembolism with a relative risk of 0.2 (95% CI 0.05-0.91).

population.label: Raschke et al randomized heparin nomogram trial participants

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 4 weight-based UFH nomogram starts with an 80-U/kg IV bolus followed by 18 U/kg/h.
The chapter states that weight-adjusted heparin dosing helps achieve therapeutic anticoagulation more rapidly and can reduce recurrent thromboembolism compared with lower fixed starting doses.
Because APTT reagent sensitivity varies, the chapter recommends adapting nomogram APTT targets to the local laboratory reagent rather than copying a universal seconds-based target.
For subcutaneous therapeutic heparin, the chapter recommends a high initial dose, with an IV bolus if a rapid effect is required, and monitoring about 6 hours after injection.
For moderate-risk prophylaxis, the chapter describes low-dose UFH 5,000 U subcutaneously two or three times daily without laboratory monitoring.
The chapter notes that evidence linking excessive APTT prolongation to bleeding was less conclusive than evidence relating inadequate anticoagulation to recurrent thrombosis.
The chapter identifies bleeding as the major complication of heparin and emphasizes avoiding excessive doses, particularly in patients with other bleeding risk factors.
In myocardial infarction studies using heparin with thrombolytic therapy, major bleeding including intracranial bleeding increased progressively when APTT values exceeded about 80 seconds.
The chapter considers short courses of heparin unlikely to cause clinically important osteoporosis but regards prolonged high-dose therapy for at least 3 months as a meaningful osteoporosis risk.
A small randomized antenatal study reported clinical osteoporosis in 1 of 20 women receiving long-term heparin prophylaxis and none of the controls.

population.label: Pregnant women in a randomized antenatal heparin prophylaxis study

atoms.canonical_statement: A randomized study reported spinal fractures in 6 of 40 patients receiving UFH 10,000 U twice daily for 3-6 months versus 1 of 40 receiving 5,000 U anti-factor Xa activity twice daily.
In a pregnancy cohort of 70 women receiving heparin, 12 (17%) had obvious radiographic osteopenia and two developed symptomatic spinal fractures postpartum.
The chapter distinguishes an early benign reversible nonimmune thrombocytopenia from the later IgG-mediated immune form of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia associated with thrombosis.
In an elective hip-surgery trial, serologically confirmed HIT occurred in about 1% by day 7 and 3% by day 14 with unfractionated heparin, versus 0% with LMWH.
Table 5 summarizes prospective therapeutic-dose heparin studies with 29 HIT cases among 978 patients (3.0%) and 9 cases of HIT plus new thrombosis (0.9%).

population.label: Patients in prospective studies receiving therapeutic-dose heparin

atoms.canonical_statement: HIT typically begins 5-15 days after starting heparin, with a reported median onset around day 10, but can occur within hours in patients exposed to heparin during the preceding months.
The review reports an odds ratio of 37 for thrombosis in HIT patients compared with patients without HIT after elective hip surgery.

population.label: Patients receiving heparin after elective hip surgery

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 6 catalogs HIT manifestations including platelet-count abnormalities, venous and arterial thrombosis, vascular occlusions, systemic reactions after IV bolus heparin, and injection-site skin reactions.
The typical platelet-count nadir in HIT is described as 20-150 × 10^9/L with a median near 50 × 10^9/L.
The chapter attributes HIT to IgG-mediated platelet activation through Fc-gamma II receptors and identifies a heparin-PF4 complex as the major target antigen.
Washed-platelet activation assays are reported to have at least 95% sensitivity and specificity for HIT when technically optimized.
In-vitro HIT assays showed frequent cross-reactivity with LMWH and substantially less cross-reactivity with danaparoid.
Table 7 provides historical anticoagulant regimens for danaparoid and ancrod as alternative treatment strategies for HIT.
The chapter notes that evidence for danaparoid and ancrod in HIT consisted of descriptive studies rather than randomized comparative trials.
Heparin-induced skin necrosis is described as the most serious heparin-associated dermal reaction and may occur with or without overt thrombocytopenia.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Case-based adverse-event evidence; no incidence denominator reported.

atoms.canonical_statement: Selective hypoaldosteronism with hyperkalemia is described as a rare but probably real adverse effect of heparin.
LMWH preparations are produced by chemical or enzymatic depolymerization of standard heparin and have a mean molecular weight around 4,000-5,000 with a distribution of about 1,000-10,000.

Commercial LMWH preparations differ in molecular-weight distribution and relative anti-factor Xa and anti-factor IIa activity and should not be assumed clinically identical solely because they belong to the same class.
LMWHs have anti-factor Xa to anti-factor IIa activity ratios reported between about 4:1 and 2:1, compared with approximately 1:1 for unfractionated heparin.
Reduced binding of LMWH to plasma proteins is described as contributing to higher bioavailability and a more predictable anticoagulant response at fixed doses.
LMWH plasma half-life is described as approximately twofold to fourfold longer than unfractionated heparin.
LMWHs are described as being cleared principally by the renal route, with prolonged biologic half-life in renal failure.
Experimental animal models summarized in the chapter generally found LMWH slightly less potent by weight than UFH but associated with substantially less bleeding at equivalent antithrombotic effects.

The chapter identifies longer half-life and more predictable weight-adjusted anticoagulant response as major LMWH advantages that permit once-daily dosing without routine laboratory monitoring in many settings.

For general-surgery prophylaxis, the chapter reports LMWH as approximately 30% more effective than UFH 5,000 U two or three times daily for preventing venous thrombosis without a difference in bleeding.

population.label: General surgical patients in randomized prophylaxis studies

concept.text: UFH 5,000 U two or three times daily

atoms.canonical_statement: In high-risk knee or hip surgery patients, the chapter reports LMWH reduced venous thrombosis by about 70% versus control without increasing bleeding.

population.label: High-risk knee or hip surgery patients

atoms.canonical_statement: The chapter concludes that LMWHs are effective for prevention and treatment of venous thrombosis and suggests their practical properties may allow selected VTE patients to be treated at home.
The chapter reports that LMWHs do not cross the placental barrier and cites descriptive pregnancy experience suggesting safety and effectiveness.
The chapter notes evidence suggesting lower rates of osteoporosis and immune thrombocytopenia with LMWH than with UFH, while warning that LMWH can cross-react in acute HIT.
The LMWH section emphasizes unresolved questions in 1995, including postoperative dose selection, osteoporosis risk, HIT cross-reactivity, interchangeability of different LMWH products, and cost.
